newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees flee Zaire warfare, U.N. to rescue staff.
newsitem.headline: Refugees flee Zaire warfare, U.N. to rescue staff.

text.p: Conflict in eastern Zaire has sent a new wave of refugees spilling through one of Africa's most violent regions, aid workers said.
A rescue plane was expected in the town of Uvira on Tuesday to evacuate U.N. and aid agency staff trapped by fighting between the Zairean army and ethnic Tutsi rebels.

The Zaire army has been battling the Banyamulenge Tutsis for more than six months but fighting has so far been largely on the high plateau above Uvira. Clashes have now spread to the plains, threatening settlements and closing most of the 100 km (60-mile) road between Uvira and Bukavu.
A senior aid official in neighbouring Burundi said 45 foreign aid workers were in danger in Uvira after attempts to evacuate them failed.

The aid workers were spending the night at United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees premises after an evacuation flight was cancelled and plans to drive in convoy to the Burundian capital were halted.
"Right now we have 45 expatriates stuck in an extremely dangerous situation," a senior aid official in Bujumbura said.
In Rome, the U.N. World Food Programme said Zairean authorities had cleared its charter to fly into Uvira.
The WFP estimated that between 44 and 54 U.N. and other aid workers were in the region, including two of its own staff.
A U.N. special envoy spent most of Monday in talks with regional officials to try and contain violence in Zaire, a country almost the size of the entire European Union.

No word leaked from the talks between the regional officials and envoy Ibrahima Fall, who is trying to prevent the conflict drawing in the armies of Burundi and Rwanda, both dominated by Tutsis. Fall arrived in Bukavu on Sunday.
Hoards of Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi were on the move in eastern Zaire on Monday in search of a safe haven from the fighting, humanitarian sources said.

The exodus coincided with reports from the U.N. refugee agency in Geneva and humanitarian sources in the region that fighting had spread from South Kivu near the border with Burundi to North Kivu and the region of Goma bordering Rwanda.
In London, Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo expressed concern about events and said neighbouring Rwanda threatened to be "a detonator for an explosion" in the sub-region.
"Unfortunately that's what it's doing," he added in remarks broadcast by the British Broadcasting Corporation.
Rwanda denied any link with the fighting after aid sources reported unidentified fighters crossing from Rwanda and attacking army positions in Zaire.
"We are not involved in operations in north or south Kivu," army spokesman Major Wilson Rutayisire said. "We are not arming the Banyamulenge."

Estimates of the size of the exodus from 12 refugee camps near Uvira by the border with Burundi ranged up to a quarter of a million. Some sources said they had taken to nearby mountains, others that they were heading for Bukavu.
There was no reliable report on the fighting or death toll.
Witnesses said Zaire had been reinforcing and resupplying its troops in the eastern refugee zone.

Banyamulenge Tutsis immigrated from Rwanda about 200 years ago. Long-running clashes between them and native Zaireans have been exarcebated by the 1994 massacres and civil war in Rwanda which created a refugee and security crisis in the region.
